content_voiceover: This slide plots dabigatran plasma concentration on the x axis against aPTT on the left and INR on the right, from Thromb Haemost 2011. Look at the aPTT panel first. As dabigatran level rises, aPTT climbs in a curvilinear fashion, moving out of the normal range shown by the orange band and continuing to rise across the therapeutic zone highlighted in blue, but it flattens out at very high concentrations. That means aPTT is a reasonable qualitative screen, useful to detect the presence of clinically relevant dabigatran, but it cannot reliably distinguish a moderately elevated level from a very high one. Now look at the INR panel on the right. INR barely moves through the therapeutic range and only rises meaningfully at supratherapeutic concentrations, so INR and PT are relatively insensitive to dabigatran and should not be relied on to exclude clinically significant drug effect. The key takeaway for boards is that a normal aPTT makes clinically important dabigatran levels unlikely, but an elevated aPTT does not tell you the actual drug concentration, and PT or INR is simply not a useful test for dabigatran.
keypoints: aPTT rises with dabigatran level but plateaus at high concentrations
PT and INR are relatively insensitive to dabigatran
A normal aPTT makes significant dabigatran effect unlikely
Neither test precisely quantifies dabigatran plasma level
